figureCaption: Projected changes in eastern redcedar habitat suitability across the Southern Great Plains under RCP4.5 and RCP8.5. Maps compare 2000–2019 with 2080–2099, and time series show the percentage of wildland area in each suitability class.
title: Projecting the future range of eastern redcedar
summary: We examined how future climate conditions may alter the distribution of eastern redcedar in the Southern Great Plains. The study projects an eastward shift in its distribution range, providing a basis for anticipating where climate suitability may change and prioritizing monitoring and management of woody encroachment.

match: Future climate change shifts the ranges
title: Anticipating range shifts of encroaching woody species
summary: We investigated how future climate change may shift the ranges of major encroaching woody plant species in the Southern Great Plains. Comparing responses among species helps identify changing areas of potential encroachment and supports planning for early intervention and grassland conservation.

match: Responses of streamflow to forest expansion
title: Connecting woody expansion with streamflow
summary: Using SWAT+ simulations in the Little River Watershed, we examined how forest expansion and future climate conditions influence streamflow. The study highlights declining water availability as forest cover increases and connects woody vegetation management with the sustainability of water resources in subhumid Oklahoma.

figureCaption: Grassland and woodland tower locations and measurement footprint contours at the Oklahoma study site. The inset shows the site's regional location.
title: Comparing juniper woodland with native tallgrass prairie
summary: We examined how the maturation of encroaching juniper woodland changes ecosystem carbon and water exchange relative to native tallgrass prairie. The study links higher gross primary productivity and water use with changes in net ecosystem exchange, demonstrating why the consequences of encroachment must be considered across multiple ecosystem processes.

figureCaption: Carbon–water trade-offs associated with increasing tree canopy cover under land use and climate change: higher evapotranspiration and net primary productivity, accompanied by lower runoff.
match: Trade-off of ecosystem productivity and water use
title: Evaluating productivity and water-use trade-offs
summary: We investigated trade-offs between ecosystem productivity and water use as tree cover increases under future climate conditions in southcentral United States. The study connects vegetation change with carbon uptake, water demand, and water-use efficiency, informing assessment of the benefits and costs of increasing woody cover.

figureCaption: Grassland and woodland carbon and water fluxes during 2022–2024: net ecosystem exchange (NEE), gross ecosystem productivity (GEP), ecosystem respiration (Re), and evapotranspiration (ET), shown alongside precipitation.
match: Sequence and Seasonal Timing of Weather Extremes
title: Understanding ecosystem stability during weather extremes
summary: Using eddy covariance observations from a central Oklahoma tallgrass prairie and an adjacent juniper-encroached woodland, we examined how the timing and sequence of wet spells and flash droughts affect carbon and water fluxes. Responses varied with vegetation type and event sequence, highlighting the importance of native grasslands for ecosystem stability under a more variable climate.
